newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian state of emergency bans gatherings.
newsitem.headline: Albanian state of emergency bans gatherings.

text.p: Albania gave security forces power to open fire to disperse crowds, restricted political activity and banned public gatherings of more than four people under a national state of emergency declared on Sunday.
The 10-article law, published by the state-run news agency ATA, was unanimously passed by parliament in response to an armed uprising spreading through the south of the impoverished Balkan state.

ATA quoted it as saying that constitutional rights and freedoms would be limited and that the army could be called in to help restore order if police and other non-military security forces were incapable of ending the anarchy.

"In the case of a state of emergency, any gathering in public places as well as activities of a political, sporting, cultural and trades union nature are prohibited," ATA quoted the legislation as saying.
"To disperse crowds, authorities can make use of tear gas and even arms if needed," the law said.
Among measures available to the authorities to enforce the state of emergency were checkpoints and roadblocks, a curfew and the posting of armed guards outside all public and state buildings.
"No more than four persons should stay together," the law says.
Parliament, controlled by President Sali Berisha's Democratic Party, passed the law in response to the most widespread unrest in Albania since the collapse of 45 years of Stalinist rule in 1990.
Two months of disturbances since the failure of high-risk pyramid investment schemes, with the loss of people's meagre savings, reached a peak of violence at the weekend.

At least 12 people were reported killed, either in clashes or by stray bullets, as demonstrators in southern towns including Vlore, Sarande and Gjirokaster raided police and army weapons depots and went on a rampage of burning and looting.
State television said parliament had also voted to merge Albania's Shik secret police organisation and the Interior Ministry, responsible for civilian police, to organise the crackdown on protests.
The combined force will be led by Shik chief General Bashkim Gazidede.

Berisha, in a televised address, vowed to use the "iron hand" of the law to crush the uprising. He blamed former communists and unspecified foreign spy services of plotting to overthrow him "and establish their rule across the country".
